title: Anatomy of a phishing email
body_md:
## Read the request, then the wrapper

A phishing email is a request dressed as a familiar message. It may ask you to sign in, open a file, pay an invoice, call a number, or share information. Its design can be polished and its spelling perfect. The useful question is: **what action does it want, and how can I check that action outside this email?**

### Work through five parts

1. **Claim.** The display name, logo and footer say who the sender wants to be. They are easy to copy. Expand the sender details and read the address, but remember that a genuine account can also be compromised. An apparently familiar address is useful context, not a verdict.
2. **Trigger.** A deadline, account warning or unexpected reward is meant to move you quickly. Real organizations also send urgent notices. Pause because the action matters, not because urgency alone proves fraud.
3. **Requested action.** Mark every link, attachment, reply address and phone number the message wants you to use. A message with no link can still steer you to a fraudulent phone line. Never send a password or one-time code in a reply.
4. **Destination.** On a desktop, hover without clicking if your client shows the URL. The visible text of a button is not its destination. If the destination is shortened, cut off or unclear, do not resolve it by following the message. A preview can show only the first hop; check the address again if you independently reach a page.
5. **Independent route.** Open the service's app or a bookmark you already use, or contact it through a number you found separately. If the claimed issue is real, you can usually see or ask about it there. For a workplace request, use your established internal channel.

Do not treat a single feature as a magic test. Authentication indicators in some mail clients can help, but they do not prove that the request is authorized. Equally, a marketing platform may send a real message from a domain different from the brand's main domain. The safe decision is about the requested action and a separate path to verify it.

### A short routine

Say the claim aloud: “This message says my account needs attention.” Then set the message aside, go through a known route, and compare the claim. If you cannot verify now, defer the action. You do not owe an unexpected email an immediate answer.

widget_config.goal: For an unexpected email, identify the requested action and verify its claim through a channel you already trust.
widget_config.today_action: Choose one recent service notification in your inbox without opening its links. Locate the sender details and decide where you would verify its claim independently.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: urgent storage warning
blocks.situation: A polished email labelled “Cloud Desk” says storage will close tonight. Its sender is help@cloud-desk-alerts.example and the button says “Keep files.” It asks for a sign-in and a one-time code.
blocks.analysis: The loss threat and code request make the proposed action high risk. The name and layout do not authenticate it. Leave the button alone; open your usual storage app or bookmarked site to inspect the account and report the message if unverified.

blocks.title: Synthetic case: real ticket change
blocks.situation: You booked a train yesterday. An email from a ticketing platform you recognize says the departure platform changed. It includes a view-ticket button and a booking reference.
blocks.analysis: The timing and reference fit a legitimate notice, yet either could be copied. Open the ticket in the app you used to buy it, or check the operator's official service page. If the change appears there, you can act without trusting the email link.

blocks.title: A mailbox decision, not a logo contest
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise. You receive an invoice email for a software subscription. No real message or account is used.

steps.prompt: The display name matches the service, but the bill was unexpected. First move?

choices.text: Open the attachment to see whether it is real.
choices.consequence: The file runs or opens before you know its origin.
choices.explanation: Unexpected files can be the payload. Inspect the claim before opening them.

choices.text: Identify the claim and set the attachment aside.
choices.consequence: You retain the evidence and avoid immediate exposure.
choices.explanation: Start with what the email wants you to do.

steps.prompt: The message says payment failed and offers a support phone number. How do you verify?

choices.text: Call the number printed in the email.
choices.consequence: The call may go to whoever authored the message.
choices.explanation: A copied footer can contain an attacker-controlled number.

choices.text: Open your existing subscription app or bookmarked account page.
choices.consequence: You can check billing through a separately established route.
choices.explanation: Independent navigation tests the claim without using the offered path.

steps.prompt: Later, you check the real account through your bookmark. It shows no unpaid invoice. What now?

choices.text: Reply asking the sender to explain.
choices.explanation: A reply does not establish identity and may invite more pressure.

choices.text: Report the suspicious email in your mail client or workplace flow.
choices.consequence: The message is sent to the relevant review channel.
choices.explanation: Report the discrepancy; do not promise that a report instantly blocks every copy.

steps.prompt: A colleague says they received the same email. How do you help?

choices.text: Forward the live email so they can inspect it.
choices.consequence: A working link or attachment reaches another inbox.
choices.explanation: Use your organization's reporting channel; avoid distributing active payloads.

choices.text: Tell them the claim was unverified and point them to the established reporting route.
choices.consequence: They can check their own account and report their copy.
choices.explanation: This gives a safe next action without spreading the message.

blocks.debrief: The email's polish and a familiar name did not settle the invoice. Independent account status did. Retry any decision to see where the email tried to move you.

questions.prompt: A message from a familiar address asks for a one-time sign-in code. What is safest?

choices.text: Send the code because the address is familiar.
choices.explanation: The account or address may be misused; a code can authorize access.

choices.text: Do not send the code; verify the request through your usual channel.
choices.explanation: The requested action is unsafe even when the wrapper looks familiar.

questions.prompt: A well-written alert says you must update payment details tonight. What does the good grammar prove?

choices.text: It proves the alert is genuine.
choices.explanation: Polished text is easy to produce.

choices.text: Nothing about authorization; check billing through the known app or site.

questions.prompt: A genuine-looking ticket update arrives just after your purchase. What should you do?

choices.text: Check your ticket in the app or operator site you already use.
choices.explanation: A plausible message can still be verified without its link.

choices.text: Assume it is false because real notices never contain buttons.
choices.explanation: Legitimate messages often contain buttons; the button is simply not your verification channel.

questions.prompt: A suspicious email has no link but tells you to call its support number. Is it safe?

choices.explanation: A phone number can be the attacker's destination.

choices.text: No conclusion yet; find the service's number independently.
choices.explanation: A call request deserves the same channel check.
